scenes.tts: One of the most-used pieces of notation in biochemistry began as a typographic fix. Measuring hydrogen ions threw off columns of decimals, written out and recompared until the bookkeeping itself became the bottleneck, so a brewery chemist compressed the mess into a logarithm. He did not think he had discovered anything.
scenes.visual: portrait inset; pH notation, decimals column through bottleneck, brewery chemist, compressed to a logarithm, not a discovery

scenes.tts: Across more than 160 pages laid out electrode by electrode, indicator by indicator, the choice that would outlast him appears exactly once, without emphasis: "For the number representing the exponent of this power, I have chosen the symbol pH." Two lowercase letters, buried.
scenes.visual: stack of 160+ pages, electrode/indicator, one highlighted line holds the quote, pH buried

scenes.tts: What his measurements did show, and what he did underline, was that enzymes do not care how much acid is present in total — only about the concentration of free protons.

scenes.tts: He proved it on the same invertase reaction that had defeated Victor Henri, whose earlier results were leaky because no pH scale yet existed to fix the acidity. Plotted on Sørensen's new logarithmic axis, the data showed a sharp activity peak the old units had hidden.
